title: Giving and offerings
question: How should a faith app ask for gifts, and what should it never promise?
lede: “Each one should give what he has decided in his heart to give, not out of regret or compulsion. For God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Corinthians 9:7). Giving is worship, and it pays for churches, missions and the apps people pray with. More of it now happens on a phone: in a church’s app, through a QR code during the service, or with a Give button in a Bible app. The design decides what is chosen for the giver, where the ask appears and what a gift is said to do. Most people who give through an app want it to be simple and safe. Design also for the person who is short of money this month, and for the one who has just told the app about their grief.
calling: Make room for cheerful giving: let people give what they decided in their heart, tell them truly what it does, and say when it is enough.

spectrum.title: From the giver’s choice to the app’s

working_example.situation: The same faith app, made by a small ministry and used by members of St Luke’s church, handles giving in seven ways. Choose who is giving: someone who gives every month, someone who installed the app this week, someone short of money this month, or someone who has just shared a prayer request. Then look at where the ask appears, the screen where they give, and what happens afterwards. Nothing is paid.

options.name: Giving stays with the church
options.origin: Familiar from churches where the offering, a bank transfer or church tax carries giving, and from Startblock’s support page, which asks first for prayer and help, then gives a bank account and a receipt on request; see the screenshot below. The church and wording here are written for this example.
options.makes_easier: Nothing in the app asks for money.
options.costs: Nothing pays for the app, and some people want to give there.
options.ask_your_team: Who pays for this app, and do its users know?

options.name: A quiet way to give
options.origin: Observed in YouVersion, captured 11 October 2026: Give from the profile, an amount that starts at zero, a regular gift switched off, and a choice between YouVersion and Bible translation; see the screenshots below. The ministry, funds and wording here are written for this example.
options.makes_easier: Easy to find when someone wants it, and silent otherwise.
options.costs: Easy to miss, and it raises less than an ask.
options.ask_your_team: Where would someone look for this, and is it there?

options.name: The church’s offering
options.origin: Observed in Churchome, captured 11 October 2026: Give in the menu, named funds, Pushpay, Apple Pay or PayPal, and a recurring gift changed in the person’s Pushpay account; see the screenshots below. Church giving apps such as Givelify (101K ratings), Church Center and Tithe.ly work the same way. In Germany congregations show a QR code during the service that leads to their own donation form. The church, funds and fee here are written for this example.
options.gain: To their own church, by fund
options.makes_easier: The gift goes to the person’s own church, by fund, with a receipt.
options.costs: Card fees, and the church’s giving records held by a platform.
options.ask_your_team: Does the giver see the fee, and who keeps their giving history?

options.name: A regular gift
options.origin: Observed in YouVersion’s “Become a Sower”, a monthly gift switched off until the person turns it on, and in Abide’s donate sheet with “Make it a monthly donation” unticked; see the screenshots below. Recurring giving is 35% of digital church giving in one vendor’s data. The reminder before a change is a proposal.
options.makes_easier: Steady support the person chose, on a day they chose.
options.costs: Easy to forget that it is running.
options.ask_your_team: Is stopping as easy as starting, and when does the giver hear about it?

options.name: What a gift does
options.origin: Observed in YouVersion’s Sowers page, a slider from $10 to $100 a month with Bibles per year beside it, and Pray as you go’s “80%” of a donation going to content; see the screenshots below. The figures here are written for this example.
options.makes_easier: People see where the money goes and what it makes possible.
options.costs: Figures age, and a number per dollar can promise too much.
options.ask_your_team: Could you show the source and the date of every figure?

options.name: A gift tied to a benefit
options.origin: Observed in Pray.com’s “Support & Go Ad Free”, where a ministry donation brings “an Ad Free Subscription”, and Glorify’s “Pay it Forward” tiers with “Most popular” ticked; see the screenshots below. Apple treats a gift tied to content as a purchase. The tiers here are written for this example.
options.cost: A price dressed as a gift
options.makes_easier: People who would pay anyway support others too.
options.costs: A purchase dressed as a gift, with a tier chosen for the giver.
options.ask_your_team: Is this a gift or a price, and would the receipt say which?

options.name: Pressure and promises
options.origin: A warning case. Evangelical theologians at Lausanne described prosperity teaching that promises health and wealth through the “sowing of seeds” in tithes and offerings; regulators objected to a default “tip” added to gifts. The seed, the countdown, the tip and the ask after a prayer request here are written for this example to show the pattern; no app is named.
options.costs: Trades on faith, fear and need, and promises what God has not.
options.ask_your_team: Would you say this to the person’s face, in your own name?

takeaways.heading: Start with no amount, and a one-off gift
takeaways.text: YouVersion’s give screen starts at zero with its monthly gift switched off; Churchome’s opens with $100.00 already filled in, and Abide’s donate sheet offers six amounts with $50 already chosen and a monthly box left unticked. An empty amount leaves the decision to the giver; if you suggest amounts, choose none in advance.

takeaways.heading: Name who receives the gift, and what it pays for
takeaways.text: YouVersion asks whether a gift goes to the app or to Bible translation; Bible.is asks people to “Donate online” for recordings in oral cultures. Say which organisation receives the money, what it pays for, and whether a receipt follows.

takeaways.heading: Keep the ask out of prayer, grief and crisis
takeaways.text: Giving belongs in a menu, after a service or on its own page, not between a prayer request and the next screen. Someone who has just written about their grief, or is in danger, should see help and nothing else.

takeaways.heading: Keep gifts and purchases apart
takeaways.text: Pray.com’s “Support & Go Ad Free” gives donors “an Ad Free Subscription”, and Glorify’s “Pay it Forward” ticks “Most popular” in advance. If a payment unlocks something, call it a price; if it is a gift, let it unlock nothing.

takeaways.heading: Stopping is as easy as starting
takeaways.text: Keep every regular gift in one place, with its next date, and let it be changed or stopped there in one step. Churchome sends people to “your Pushpay account” to change one: say where, and link to it. Remind the giver before a yearly gift or a change in amount.

takeaways.heading: Say what a gift does, truly, and when enough is enough
takeaways.text: YouVersion’s Sowers page sets Bibles per year beside a monthly amount; Pray as you go says 80% of a donation goes to its content. Give each figure a source and a date, and when a need is met, say so, as Moses did.

takeaways.heading: Never promise a return
takeaways.text: A gift is not a seed that obliges God to send a harvest. Leave out anything that ties a gift to healing, prosperity, answered prayer or a blessing, and anything that ranks givers or shows who gave what.

research.subtitle: Given freely, in secret, as one is able

findings.heading: Decided in the heart
findings.text: “Each one should give what he has decided in his heart to give, not out of regret or compulsion” (2 Corinthians 9:7); “the gift is acceptable according to what one has, not according to what he does not have” (2 Corinthians 8:12). The poor widow’s two coins were “more than all the others” (Mark 12:43).

findings.heading: In secret, and set aside
findings.text: “When you give to the needy, do not let your left hand know what your right hand is doing, so that your giving may be in secret” (Matthew 6:3–4). Paul asked each to “set aside a portion of his income” “on the first day of every week” (1 Corinthians 16:2): a regular gift, planned, not pressed out at the moment of asking.

findings.heading: Handled openly, and enough is enough
findings.text: Paul took “great care to do what is right, not only in the eyes of the Lord but also in the eyes of men” in handling a gift (2 Corinthians 8:21). When the people brought more than was needed for the tabernacle, which Bezalel built, Moses “sent a proclamation throughout the camp” and “the people were restrained from bringing more” (Exodus 36:6).

findings.heading: Tithe, offering and church tax
findings.text: Christians give in different ways: a tenth, as Israel brought “the full tithe into the storehouse” (Malachi 3:10); a proportion “as he is able” (Deuteronomy 16:17); weekly offerings; or, in Germany, church tax collected with income tax. Jesus did not set the tithe aside but named “justice, mercy and faithfulness” as weightier (Matthew 23:23).

research.subtitle: What the stores, regulators and tax offices ask

findings.heading: A gift, or a purchase
findings.text: On iPhone, “Approved nonprofits may fundraise directly within their own apps”, with Apple Pay, and “must disclose how the funds will be used”; others “may only collect funds outside of the app”. A gift “connected to or associated at any point in time with receiving digital content or services must use in-app purchase”. Google Play exempts “tax exempt donations” from its billing.

findings.heading: Pressure has a name
findings.text: The UK Code of Fundraising Practice requires “not putting undue pressure on a person to donate, not using unreasonably persistent approaches and accepting a request to end an interaction”. In 2026 US state regulators objected to “the application of a default “tip” that went directly to GoFundMe”.

findings.heading: Receipts belong to the gift
findings.text: In the US, organisations give a written acknowledgment for “contributions of $250 or more”, which may say that “the organization only provided intangible religious benefits”. A UK Gift Aid declaration must explain that “the donor is responsible to pay any difference”.

findings.heading: Current, complete and accurate
findings.text: Christian ministries in the ECFA agreed that what they tell donors “must be current, complete and accurate”, that past events “must be appropriately dated”, and that appeals “must not create unrealistic donor expectations of what a donor’s gift will actually accomplish”.

research.subtitle: What defaults, recognition and promises do

findings.heading: A suggested amount moves people
findings.text: Goswami and Urminsky found “a scale-back effect, in which low defaults reduce average donation amounts”, and “a lower-bar effect, in which defaulting a low amount increases donation rate”. Any default also weakened “other cues such as positive charity information”.

findings.heading: Being seen raises gifts
findings.text: In a field experiment, “charitable gifts increase in response to the promise of public recognition primarily because of individuals’ desire to improve their social image”: the motive Jesus warned against in Matthew 6.

findings.heading: Much church giving is now digital
findings.text: Churches that offer digital giving “reported that 41% of their giving came from digital methods”, and “Recurring giving accounted for 35% of the digital giving in 2025”, in one vendor’s US data. Givelify, the giving app with the most ratings (101K), says it “has processed $6 billion in donations”. In Württemberg almost 400 congregations take the collection through a QR code and a web form.

findings.heading: Seeds and harvests
findings.text: Evangelical theologians at Lausanne described prosperity teaching that promises health and wealth through “the “sowing of seeds” through the faithful payments of tithes and offerings”, and warned against “Replacing the traditional call to repentance and faith with a call to give money”.

which_fits.start_with: The church’s offering: funds, a receipt, a QR code at the service, fees shown

which_fits.if: A Bible or prayer app run by a ministry
which_fits.start_with: A quiet way to give, a regular gift if chosen, honest figures
What a gift does, with every figure sourced and dated

which_fits.if: An app that also sells a subscription
which_fits.start_with: Keep the price and the gift apart; let a gift unlock nothing

which_fits.if: You are tempted to add a seed, a countdown or an ask after a prayer request
which_fits.start_with: Don’t: let people give what they decided in their heart

reflection.heading: What giving is for
reflection.text: “Who am I, and who are my people, that we should be able to give as generously as this? For everything comes from You, and from Your own hand we have given to You” (1 Chronicles 29:14). Giving returns to God what was already his, supports those who serve the word, and cares for those in need. Jesus said that “It is more blessed to give than to receive” (Acts 20:35), and looked not at the size of a gift but at what it cost the giver.

reflection.heading: Where Christians differ
reflection.text: Some churches teach the tithe as the measure of faithful giving; others teach proportional giving “as he is able” (Deuteronomy 16:17) and see the tithe as a starting point or as Israel’s law. Catholics give through the offertory, Mass offerings and parish appeals; in Germany church tax carries most church income and the collection is for a named cause. Pentecostal and charismatic churches range from careful teaching on stewardship to the prosperity teaching that the Lausanne statement rejected. All agree that a gift is free, and that those who receive it must handle it honestly.

reflection.heading: What follows for design
reflection.text: Let people give what they decided in their heart: nothing chosen for them, nothing asked in a moment of need. Say who receives the gift and what it truly does, keep it in secret unless the giver chooses otherwise, and make a regular gift easy to stop. Never promise a return, and when the need is met, say so.

voices.source: Henri Nouwen, A Spirituality of Fundraising (2010)
voices.note: wrote that “Fundraising is first and foremost a ministry”, “a way of announcing our vision and inviting other people into our mission”, and “precisely the opposite of begging”.
told Methodists to “gain all you can”, “save all you can” and “give all you can”: giving is the end that earning and saving serve.

three_ways.exploitative: Choose the amount and the tier for the giver, switch on monthly by default, add a tip unless it is removed, ask after a prayer request, and promise a harvest for a seed.
three_ways.ethical: Start with no amount and a one-off gift, name who receives it and what it pays for, show fees, send receipts, and let a regular gift be stopped in one step.
three_ways.redemptive: Ask only where people look for it, never in prayer, grief or need; give every figure a source and a date, say when enough has been given, and give up the gifts that pressure would bring.

decide.question: What is chosen for the giver, where does the ask appear, and what does the app say a gift will do?
decide.exercise: Give the smallest gift your app allows, three times: as someone new, as someone who has just lost their job, and as someone who has just shared a prayer request. Write down every amount, tick and toggle chosen for you, and every place the ask appeared. Set up a regular gift and time how long it takes to stop it. Then read every sentence about what a gift will do aloud to a member of your church who gives faithfully and has little, and ask whether you would say it to their face.

sources.title: App Store Review Guidelines: 3.2.1 (vi) and (vii), 3.2.2 (iv)
sources.author: Apple
sources.shows: “Approved nonprofits may fundraise directly within their own apps or third-party apps, provided those fundraising campaigns … offer Apple Pay support”; they “must disclose how the funds will be used” and “ensure appropriate tax receipts are available to donors”. Others “may only collect funds outside of the app, such as via Safari or SMS”. A gift “connected to or associated at any point in time with receiving digital content or services must use in-app purchase”.
sources.application: On iPhone, a gift is either a gift to an approved nonprofit, with Apple Pay, or collected outside the app; a gift that unlocks content is a purchase.
sources.limits: Rules for one platform; they change, and approval as a nonprofit is a separate process.

sources.title: Payments policy (Google Play)
sources.author: Google Play Console Help
sources.shows: Google Play’s billing is not required where “payments include peer-to-peer payments, online auctions, and tax exempt donations”.
sources.application: On Android, donations to tax-exempt organisations can use the organisation’s own payment provider.
sources.limits: A summary page of a longer policy; the exemption depends on the organisation’s status.

sources.title: When Should the Ask Be a Nudge? The Effect of Default Amounts on Charitable Donations
sources.author: Indranil Goswami and Oleg Urminsky · Journal of Marketing Research, 2016
sources.shows: Finds “a scale-back effect, in which low defaults reduce average donation amounts”, “a lower-bar effect, in which defaulting a low amount increases donation rate”, and “a default-distraction effect, in which introducing any defaults reduces the effect of other cues such as positive charity information”.
sources.application: A suggested amount changes who gives and how much; an empty field leaves the decision to the giver.
sources.limits: Charity appeals, not church giving; effects vary with the amounts tested.

sources.title: Hey Look at Me: The Effect of Giving Circles on Giving
sources.author: Dean Karlan and Margaret A. McConnell · NBER working paper 17737, 2012
sources.shows: A field experiment with donors to a Yale University service club: “charitable gifts increase in response to the promise of public recognition primarily because of individuals’ desire to improve their social image”.
sources.application: Showing givers to others raises giving, and does so through the motive Jesus warned against.
sources.limits: One university club in the United States.

sources.title: 2026 Protestant Annual Church Giving Report
sources.author: Ministry Brands, 2026
sources.shows: Churches that offer digital giving “reported that 41% of their giving came from digital methods”; “Recurring giving accounted for 35% of the digital giving in 2025”.
sources.application: Much church giving is now digital, and a third of it is regular.
sources.limits: A survey of church leaders and data from one vendor’s customers in the United States; the vendor sells giving software.

sources.title: ECFA Standards for Fund Raising
sources.author: Evangelical Council for Financial Accountability · Christianity Today, May 1987
sources.shows: Representations “must be current, complete and accurate. References to past activities or events must be appropriately dated”; “Fund raising appeals must not create unrealistic donor expectations of what a donor’s gift will actually accomplish”.
sources.application: A figure about what a gift does needs a date, a source and an honest scope.
sources.limits: The 1987 published standards; ECFA’s current wording is longer, with the same principle.

sources.title: A Statement on the Prosperity Gospel
sources.author: Lausanne Theology Working Group, Africa chapter · 2008–2009, published January 2010
sources.shows: Defines prosperity teaching as obtaining health and wealth “through positive confessions of faith and the “sowing of seeds” through the faithful payments of tithes and offerings”, and lists among its effects “Replacing the traditional call to repentance and faith with a call to give money”.
sources.application: An ask that promises return for a gift has been named and rejected by evangelical churches worldwide.
sources.limits: A statement from evangelical theologians; it also affirms a biblical vision of human flourishing.

sources.title: Code of Fundraising Practice 2025: table of changes
sources.author: Fundraising Regulator (UK)
sources.shows: Fundraising must include “not putting undue pressure on a person to donate, not using unreasonably persistent approaches and accepting a request to end an interaction”.
sources.application: Pressure and persistence are named limits in UK fundraising, and churches that are charities are within its scope.
sources.limits: A UK self-regulatory code; wording is from the 2025 revision.

sources.title: Bipartisan group of state attorneys general and state charity regulators send letter to GoFundMe
sources.author: Crowell & Moring client alert, March 2026
sources.shows: Among the concerns in the regulators’ letter: “the application of a default “tip” that went directly to GoFundMe”.
sources.application: A tip added by default to a gift is a regulatory concern, not only a design choice.
sources.limits: A law firm’s summary of the letter; GoFundMe disputed some of the regulators’ points.

sources.title: Publication 1771: Charitable Contributions, Substantiation and Disclosure Requirements
sources.author: Internal Revenue Service (US)
sources.shows: Organisations that receive “contributions of $250 or more” give a written acknowledgment, which can state that “the organization only provided intangible religious benefits”.
sources.application: A receipt is part of giving; a gift that buys something, such as an ad-free app, is acknowledged differently.
sources.limits: US tax rules; other countries differ.

sources.title: Gift Aid declarations: claiming tax back on donations
sources.author: HM Revenue & Customs (UK)
sources.shows: A declaration must tell donors that they need to pay enough UK tax to cover what charities claim, and that “the donor is responsible to pay any difference”.
sources.application: A tick box for Gift Aid needs its explanation, not only a pre-ticked box.

sources.title: Mehr Spenden in Baden-Württemberg: Kirchen testen digitale Kollekte
sources.author: Wochenblatt-Reporter
sources.shows: Congregations show QR codes on hymn sheets, posters or during the service, leading to the congregation’s online donation form; in Württemberg “knapp 400 Gemeinden und kirchliche Einrichtungen” have set up such forms.
sources.application: In German churches the digital collection is mostly a QR code to a web form, not an app.
sources.limits: A regional news report; church tax still carries most church income in Germany.

sources.title: Givelify Mobile Giving App (App Store listing)
sources.author: Givelify · Apple App Store (US)
sources.shows: “#1 App to Donate, Tithe & Give”, with 101K ratings, 4.9.
sources.application: The one giving app with reach of its own; most church giving apps are white-label apps in each church’s name.

sources.title: Led by Dallas entrepreneur, Givelify reports $300 million in North Texas giving, $6 billion globally
sources.author: David Seeley · Dallas Innovates, 1 October 2025
sources.shows: The company says it “has processed $6 billion in donations from 2 million donors supporting 75,000 nonprofits and places of worship”.
sources.application: Giving through apps is no longer marginal.

sources.title: A Spirituality of Fundraising
sources.author: Henri J. M. Nouwen · Upper Room Books, 2010
sources.shows: “Fundraising is first and foremost a ministry”: “a way of announcing our vision and inviting other people into our mission”, and “precisely the opposite of begging”.
sources.application: An ask can be an invitation into shared work, not a transaction or a plea.
sources.limits: A short book drawn from a talk; the publisher’s summary is quoted here.

sources.title: TelefonSeelsorge
sources.author: TelefonSeelsorge Deutschland (Protestant and Catholic churches)
sources.shows: “Tag und Nacht erreichbar 0800 1110111 / 0800 1110222 oder 116 123”, by phone, chat or email.
sources.application: A first screen can carry a way to a person, day and night, free of charge.
sources.limits: Germany; other countries have their own services.

review.what: What is shown to someone short of money or who has just shared a prayer request, the description of seed-faith appeals, the treatment of tithing and church tax, and the use of YouVersion screens from a personal account
needs: theology across Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant traditions
